summary: DHCPv4 already has a Leasequery feature for asking about one address binding at a time. That is inefficient or impractical in some cases. This standards-track RFC adds an active mode, where a requestor can ask a DHCP server for bulk binding information and keep receiving updates as bindings change. It updates RFC 6926.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking the office clerk about one visitor at a time, you get the whole guest list and the clerk keeps telling you whenever someone arrives or leaves.

questions: how to get dhcp lease updates in bulk
what does catchupcomplete mean in dhcp
subtitle: A long-lived DHCPv4 connection that streams lease changes to an outside system as they happen.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 Leasequery only answers questions about individual bindings, which is inefficient or impossible for systems that must stay current with every lease change.
tldr.mechanism: A requestor opens a TCP connection and sends a DHCPACTIVELEASEQUERY. The server then streams DHCPLEASEACTIVE and DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED messages as bindings change, and can replay recent changes after a reconnect.
tldr.outcome: Requestors get near real-time binding data but not a complete history, since only the current state of each binding is sent. Bulk Leasequery is still used to initialize a database or recover missed data.

today: RFC 7724 is a Proposed Standard from December 2015, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6926 and builds on RFC 4388.

sections.title: Why Active Leasequery
sections.content:
DHCPv4 Leasequery (RFC 4388) lets an outside entity ask a DHCPv4 server about the lease state of one IPv4 address or client. Bulk Leasequery (RFC 6926) lets an entity pull lots of binding information, for example when it starts up. Some requestors need more: they must keep up with the server's binding activity continuously. The RFC calls this Active Leasequery.

It is meant for an entity that is not directly part of the DHCPv4 client-server exchange but still has to stay current with the lease state database in near real time.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking one question at a time is slow. Active Leasequery is like leaving a phone line open so the clerk can call you each time the guest list changes.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
Active Leasequery is modeled on the individual Leasequery and Bulk Leasequery protocols. The requestor opens a TCP connection to the DHCPv4 server on port 67, so it needs the server's address and unicast reachability. No relaying is specified. It then sends a DHCPACTIVELEASEQUERY message, and the server answers with DHCPLEASEACTIVE and DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED messages whenever binding state changes. A server that supports Active Leasequery MUST also support Bulk Leasequery.

Much of the design deals with disconnection. The requestor tracks the highest base-time it has received. After reconnecting, it puts that value in a query-start-time option, and the server sends the changes since then (the catch-up information). The server MAY limit how much history it keeps. If it kept too little, it says so and the requestor falls back to Bulk Leasequery.

The intended pattern is an initial Bulk Leasequery to fill the database, then Active Leasequery to keep it current. Active Leasequery has only one qualifier (query-start-time) and no query types, and the connection never completes; the server may close it for exceptional reasons. The messages use the same encoding as Bulk Leasequery, except that a server SHOULD be configurable to withhold specific data items even if the requestor asked for them in its parameter request list.
sections.plainLanguage: If your line drops, you tell the clerk when you last heard something. The clerk then repeats what you missed. If you were gone too long, you ask for the full list again.

sections.title: New Messages, Status Codes and Timers
sections.content:
The message framing for TCP is the same as for Bulk Leasequery, and with TLS one DHCP message is carried in one TLS record. The dhcp-message-type option (option 53) gains three values: DHCPACTIVELEASEQUERY, DHCPLEASEQUERYSTATUS and DHCPTLS.

The dhcp-status-code option from RFC 6926 is reused with four new codes: DataMissing, ConnectionActive, CatchUpComplete and TLSConnectionRefused. When it appears with DHCPLEASEQUERYSTATUS it refers to the whole request stream, otherwise to a single reply.

Three timers have defaults: a 120 second receive timeout, a 120 second send timeout and a 60 second idle timeout. Implementations MAY make them configurable, but timeouts smaller than the defaults SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk and you agree on a few new signals, like "I am still here" and "you are all caught up", and on how long to wait before deciding the line is dead.

sections.title: How a Requestor Behaves
sections.content:
A requestor SHOULD be able to work in insecure or secure mode. In secure mode it MUST try to negotiate TLS: it first sends a DHCPTLS message with no options, and if the server does not answer with a plain DHCPTLS, the requestor MUST close the connection. After a successful TLS handshake it validates the server's certificates and sends the query over TLS.

An Active Leasequery request MUST NOT have a ciaddr, chaddr or dhcp-client-identifier, and MUST have an xid unique on the connection. It SHOULD include a parameter request list. Only one DHCPACTIVELEASEQUERY is allowed per TCP connection at a time. A reply carrying binding data MUST include a non-zero ciaddr, and the requestor MUST be prepared for multiple copies of the data for one address.

On an idle connection the server SHOULD send a DHCPLEASEQUERYSTATUS with ConnectionActive every idle-timeout period, so the requestor can tell the link is alive. A requestor whose reply stream stalls SHOULD terminate after the receive timeout.

If the request had a query-start-time, the connection starts in the catch-up phase. Catch-up updates are not in the order the data changed, so the requestor must not adopt a new base-time until it sees CatchUpComplete (or DataMissing). On DataMissing, the requestor SHOULD issue a Bulk Leasequery covering the gap.
sections.plainLanguage: You first check that you are talking to the right clerk, and you only write down "I have heard everything up to here" once the clerk says the catch-up is finished.

sections.title: How a Server Behaves
sections.content:
Active Leasequery MUST NOT be enabled by default and needs an explicit configuration step. Insecure mode must never be the default, and enabling it needs its own separate step. In secure mode the server MUST support TLS and be configurable about which requestors it will talk to, based on the certificate the requestor presents. All TLS connections used for Active Leasequery MUST be mutually authenticated, and the server MUST close the TCP connection if the handshake fails.

The server SHOULD send binding information with minimal delay, but it SHOULD NOT delay its reply to the DHCP client to do so. If a request carries a query-end-time option, the server should send a MalformedQuery status and terminate. To support catch-up, the server SHOULD keep, and SHOULD limit and make configurable, some record of previous binding activity. It need not keep that across a restart, or at all. Once the catch-up messages are sent it MUST send CatchUpComplete.

The server also MAY close a connection at any time, and SHOULD limit its connection count and close idle ones. When it aborts an in-process request it SHOULD send QueryTerminated and then MUST close. A blocked send SHOULD end after the send timeout. For parallel queries, an Active and a Bulk Leasequery MUST use different connections.

This RFC also updates RFC 6926: a server that receives a DHCP message type not supported over a TCP connection, such as DHCPDISCOVER, MUST close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk keeps this service off until someone turns it on, checks everyone's ID, and hangs up if a caller is rude or goes silent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general DHCPv4 threats and the Leasequery recommendations (restricting to trusted requestors, DoS mitigation, IPsec) still apply. Using TCP adds the risk of connection exhaustion: malicious requestors may open connections and send invalid, partial or no queries to use up the server's pool.

The two modes suit two use models. Secure mode (TLS) fits a requestor at an arbitrary place on the Internet, where data must be protected and both identities verified. Insecure mode is sufficient where the requestor sits next to the DHCP server inside a protected environment. Insecure mode gives no way to check that a requestor is authorized.

Servers SHOULD offer settings to limit connection sources by certificate, cap the number of connections and bound idle time. The data acquired SHOULD be protected as strongly as the server's own data and deleted as soon as possible after use.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can hold the line open could pester the clerk, so the clerk wants to know who is calling, and callers should shred the list once they are done with it.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned three message types in the DHCP Message Type 53 registry and four status codes in the DHCP Status Code Type 151 registry. The values are shown in the table above. The message types are DHCPACTIVELEASEQUERY, DHCPLEASEQUERYSTATUS and DHCPTLS, and the codes are DataMissing, ConnectionActive, CatchUpComplete and TLSConnectionRefused.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of DHCP numbers now includes the new signals so nobody else reuses them.
